title: Variables (var, let, const)
summary: Variables give values names so you can use them later.

subtopics.title: Names and values
subtopics.explanation: A declaration creates a named binding, and assignment gives that name a value. For example, `const city = "Pune"` binds text to `city`. Choose names that explain what the value represents. A variable name is a label for code readers, not a guarantee about the value’s runtime type. Prefer names that reveal the kind of value and its role. Avoid reusing one name for unrelated meanings as a function grows. The name is like a label on a storage box; assignment puts a value inside it.

subtopics.title: const and let
subtopics.explanation: `const` prevents assigning a new value to the binding. It does not freeze an object stored there: a property may still change. Use `const` when the name should keep referring to the same value. For example, a fixed page title can use `const` while a changing score cannot. Const prevents replacing the binding, not mutation of an object or array. Use immutable updates when other parts of the program depend on the old value. Think of a `const` binding as a fixed name tag: it cannot point to a different value, even if an object’s contents change.

subtopics.title: Block scope
subtopics.explanation: `let` allows a later assignment. Use it when the value intentionally changes, such as a counter or current step. Keep the variable’s scope small and update it at a clear point. If a value never needs reassignment, `const` communicates that fact more directly. Let should represent intentional change. If the value changes in many distant places, make those updates explicit so state remains understandable. Block scope is like keeping a tool inside one work area.

subtopics.title: var and modern code
subtopics.explanation: `let` and `const` are block-scoped: they are available inside the braces where they are declared. A value created inside an `if` block cannot be read afterward. This is like keeping a tool in one work area. Block scope reduces accidental name collisions. Block scope limits where the binding can be read. Declare a value near its first use and do not reach for an outer variable after its block ends.

subtopics.title: Choosing a declaration
subtopics.explanation: `var` is older and function-scoped, so a declaration inside a loop or condition may remain available across a larger function than expected. Prefer `const` and `let` in modern code. Their scope and reassignment rules make it easier to see where a value is created and used. Legacy var can be hoisted within a function, producing surprising availability before its declaration line. Use const or let to make scope more predictable. Var is like leaving a tool in a shared hallway instead of the room where it is needed.

foundations.overview: A variable gives a name to a value so code can use it later. JavaScript offers `const` and `let` for declarations; modern code usually avoids `var`. Think of a variable like a labeled slot. `const` prevents replacing the slot’s value, but it does not freeze an object stored there.
foundations.whyItMatters: Clear declarations make state changes easier to trace. Choosing const, let, and narrow scope helps prevent accidental reassignment and name collisions.
foundations.mentalModel: A variable gives a name to a value so code can use it later.
foundations.browserPerspective: When the engine enters a scope, it creates the variable bindings up front (hoisting). var bindings are immediately set to undefined; let/const bindings are created but left uninitialized until execution reaches their declaration, enforcing the temporal dead zone. The engine resolves each variable reference against this scope structure.
foundations.realWorldUsage: const for imported modules, configuration values, and references you won't reassign; let for loop counters and accumulators; var almost never in modern code. Linters and style guides (Airbnb, StandardJS) enforce 'prefer-const' and 'no-var'.
foundations.businessImpact: Predictable variable behavior reduces bugs that reach production, lowering maintenance cost. Clear naming and const-by-default make codebases easier for new hires to read and safely modify.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing scope and the TDZ prevents subtle bugs like the var-in-a-loop closure problem and use-before-declaration errors. Defaulting to const documents intent and lets tools catch accidental reassignment.
foundations.performanceImpact: The choice rarely affects raw performance, but block scoping can help engines and developers reason about variable lifetimes, and const signals immutability that can aid readability and refactoring safety more than speed.
commonUseCases: Declaring values that never change with const (config, references)
Loop counters and accumulators with let
Holding intermediate results in a calculation
Naming function results to make code self-documenting

commonMisconceptions.myth: const makes the value completely immutable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: const only prevents reassigning the variable; objects and arrays it points to can still be mutated. Use Object.freeze for deep immutability.

commonMisconceptions.myth: let and const are not hoisted.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are hoisted, but not initialized — using them before their declaration throws a ReferenceError due to the temporal dead zone.

commonMisconceptions.myth: var, let, and const are interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ in scope, reassignment, redeclaration, and hoisting behavior; using var can introduce bugs that let/const prevent.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Const makes every object property immutable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Const protects the binding from reassignment; the object may still be mutable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Let and var both have block scope.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Let is block-scoped, while var is function-scoped and can behave unexpectedly.

visualExplorer.title: var vs. let vs. const through a scope
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how each keyword behaves as the engine enters a block and runs the code.

config.intro: Watch how declaration, hoisting, scope, and reassignment differ across var, let, and const.

steps.name: Enter the scope
steps.detail: The engine hoists all declarations: var is set to undefined, let/const are created but uninitialized (TDZ begins).

steps.name: Use before declaration
steps.detail: Reading a var gives undefined; reading a let/const throws a ReferenceError while in the TDZ.

steps.name: Reach the declaration line
steps.detail: let/const become initialized; const must be given a value right here.

steps.name: Reassign
steps.detail: var and let can be reassigned; const throws a TypeError if you try.

steps.name: Mutate an object
steps.detail: Even a const object can have its properties changed — const locks the binding, not the contents.

steps.name: Leave a block
steps.detail: let/const declared inside the block disappear; a var leaks out to the surrounding function.

interactiveExamples.title: let can change, const cannot
interactiveExamples.explanation: A let variable can be reassigned to a new value; attempting to reassign a const throws a TypeError. This is why we wrap the const reassignment in a try/catch to show the error.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: score: 20, then an Error about assignment to constant variable.

interactiveExamples.title: Block scope vs. function scope
interactiveExamples.explanation: var leaks out of the block it was declared in, while let stays contained. Reading the let outside its block throws a ReferenceError.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: I escaped, then an Error that trapped is not defined.

interactiveExamples.title: const objects are still mutable
interactiveExamples.explanation: You can change the properties of a const object because const only locks the binding. Reassigning the whole object, however, throws.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The updated user object, then an Error about assignment to constant variable.

codeLab.title: Refactor var to const/let
codeLab.instructions: The starter uses var for everything. Refactor so values that never change use const and the accumulator uses let. Keep the output the same: the sum of the prices.
hints: Use const for the array since the binding never changes.
Use let for the accumulator and the loop counter because they are reassigned.

keyTakeaways: A declaration creates a named binding, and assignment gives that name a value.
`const` prevents assigning a new value to the binding.
`let` and `const` are block-scoped: they are available inside the braces where they are declared.
`var` is older and function-scoped, so a declaration inside a loop or condition may remain available across a larger function than expected.
